messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Downward Comparison: I remind myself it could have been worse, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

Vignette:
Amina is a 47-year-old architect who has spent two decades designing buildings, overseeing construction sites, and walking through frameworks of steel and concrete with the easy confidence of someone who knows the language of structures. Seven months ago, on a Tuesday morning, she was standing on the fifth floor of a commercial project in downtown Atlanta, reviewing the placement of a steel beam with the crane operator. She gave the standard hand signal to lower—a gesture she had made hundreds of times before—but the load shifted unexpectedly, and the beam swung sideways, catching a young carpenter named Marcus across the back as he turned to check his harness. She heard the crack of bone, then his scream, and then the wet, metallic taste of her own mouth as she ran toward him, because in that moment the air was full of dust and the sound of the alarm, and she could taste it all.

In the weeks that followed, Amina found she could not deliberately bring the event to mind. When her husband, David, asked what exactly she had seen, she felt a wall inside her head—a blur of shapes and sounds that would not come into focus. But the memory did not need her permission. At night, lying in bed, she would suddenly hear the clang of the beam and Marcus’s voice, as if someone had pressed play inside her ear. And then, without warning, the taste would return: the chalky, gritty dust mixed with her own saliva, so real that she would have to spit into a tissue. She began to believe that if she caught herself performing a mental ritual—counting backward from ten in sets of three, or reciting the names of everyone who had been on the site that morning in the correct order—then nothing like that would ever happen again. She knew, logically, that counting could not undo what had already occurred, but the relief she felt after completing a ritual was too powerful to ignore. If she skipped a sequence, she would feel a spike of dread that lasted hours.

At work, she stopped going to site inspections. She told her partners she wanted to focus on design, but the truth was that every sound on a construction site—the hiss of a welder, the thud of a dropped hammer—sent her heart racing. She would jolt at the sound of her own ringtone if it was set to a tone she had heard that morning. David began to notice that she would flinch when he opened a can of soda, the pop making her spill coffee. She had trouble concentrating during client meetings, losing track of sentences halfway through. She started telling herself that somebody else—a better architect, a more careful person—would not have gotten into that situation. She dwelled on what she had done wrong: maybe her signal was ambiguous, maybe she should have checked the rigging herself. The shame built until she felt as though the person she had become—the rigid, jumpy, exhausted woman who counted in her head at stoplights—was unrecognisable. She avoided her old friends from the construction industry because she was certain they would see the guilt written on her face. She felt isolated and set apart from everyone, even David, who kept saying, “It was an accident,” a phrase she had come to hate because it suggested she should move on, and she could not.

She came to the clinic because David had found her standing in the kitchen at three in the morning, whispering numbers under her breath. She was afraid of what she would become if she did not get help. But what she said aloud, staring at her hands, was: “I just want to stop tasting the dust.”

missing_explanations: The vignette does not include the patient reminding herself that it could have been worse; instead it includes a comparison to a better architect (upward comparison).
